doc.title: Earl May interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 11, 2001

chapter: Gloria Lynne, Milt Hinton and later work
title: Playing with Gloria Lynne
summary: May worked with Gloria Lynne from late 1959 to about 1964 in a close quartet until she left the trio.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left

blocks.x: How did this — you did some things with Gloria Lynne was it?

Yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah. That was a lot of fun too, because I had a lot to do with the music. When I say that I mean I don’t write or anything, I don’t have that kind of technique or anything, but I’d come up with some ideas every once in a while, you know, where I would say, “Hey, let’s start this tune—” where the introduction would be a rim shot [sings] bop — I see your face before me. Little dumb things like that I mean they weren’t dumb but we have a lot of fun though. It was wonderful.

This was late 50s, right after Billy Taylor. I stayed with Billy from ’51 to about late ’59, and then I started with Gloria right after that, late ’59 into the 60s, up to about ’64 maybe. I’m sorry it didn’t last longer than that but it wasn’t my fault. But we had Herman Foster and Russell Elefante. And the compliments we got was that it actually was like if you saw one you would see the other three of us. The four of us. The trio and her. And we were very close, very, very — like I say you wouldn’t see one without the other four. And then people would come in, when you’re starting to reach a little success, people come in from the woodwork and they say, “Ah, man, you don’t need this person, he’s not doing anything, he’s pimping off you” or something like that. The piano player’s blind, he can’t see, and you don’t need the drummer, he can’t read music. You don’t need any of them. Come on and go with me. I’m going to put you in rooms that have dollar bills painted all over the walls. And she went for it. You know.
Oh yeah. She became quite the pop—

It can happen. So that broke that up, which was kind of sad. Because we all had dreams of staying together as long as the Modern Jazz Quartet or Gladys Knight and the Pips, you know staying together for thirty-five, forty years or something like that.
